goal: Arduino Uno parking sensor: an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (TRIG on D7, ECHO on D6, VCC 5V, GND) and a piezo buzzer on D8 that beeps faster as an object gets closer, plus a red 5 mm LED on D13 through a 220 ohm resistor that lights under 10 cm.

plan.title: Arduino Uno Parking Sensor
plan.summary: The ultrasonic sensor measures the distance to an object, and a passive piezo buzzer beeps faster as it gets closer. A red LED lights when the measured distance is under 10 cm; beeping stops beyond 100 cm or when no echo is detected.
plan.final_result: The finished breadboard has one red LED and resistor near row 10, the ultrasonic sensor near rows 24–27, and the piezo near rows 40–43, with nine jumper wires. With the sketch running, an object within 100 cm produces short beeps that become more frequent as it approaches. Below 10 cm the external red LED lights; the Uno's built-in pin-13 LED may light too. No echo or a distance beyond 100 cm produces silence and an unlit warning LED.
safety: Keep USB and any other power disconnected while placing or changing components.
Before applying USB power, verify the sensor's printed VCC and GND labels and check that 5V is not connected to the ground rail.
Keep the 220 ohm resistor in series with the LED; never connect the LED directly between D13 and ground.
Use a low-current passive piezo suitable for direct Arduino GPIO drive. A magnetic buzzer, speaker or higher-current sounder requires a driver circuit instead.
Do not force a sensor header with a different pin order into this layout; the printed labels must match the listed placements.
The HC-SR04 has a minimum useful range of about 2 cm and may miss angled, soft or narrow objects. This is a learning project, not a vehicle safety system.

part_guide.breadboard: The white board with numbered rows holds leads without solder. Within each row, holes a through e connect together, separately from f through j.
part_guide.uno: The blue-green Arduino board has a USB-B socket and labelled black pin headers. It measures the echo pulse and controls the warnings.
part_guide.led_red: The red round LED is the close-distance warning. Its longer leg is positive; its shorter leg and the flat side of its rim identify the negative side.
part_guide.resistor_led: The small beige component with red, red, brown and usually gold bands is a 220 ohm resistor. It limits LED current and works either way round.
part_guide.sensor: The HC-SR04 has two silver cylinders like eyes and four labelled pins. One cylinder sends ultrasound and the other receives its echo.
part_guide.buzzer: The small black passive piezo produces sound from the Arduino's tone signal. Find its positive lead using the + marking, rather than guessing from lead length alone.
part_guide.wire_ground: This black jumper joins Arduino GND to the first hole of the top-edge ground rail. It gives every component a shared electrical reference.
part_guide.wire_led_signal: This orange jumper runs from pin 13 to the LED's positive row. It carries the on/off warning signal.
part_guide.wire_led_ground: This black jumper runs upward from the resistor's free end to the ground rail. It completes the LED circuit.
part_guide.wire_sensor_power: This red jumper joins the Arduino 5V header to the sensor's VCC row. It powers the ultrasonic sensor.
part_guide.wire_sensor_trig: This yellow jumper joins pin 7 to the sensor's Trig row. A short pulse on this wire starts each measurement.
part_guide.wire_sensor_echo: This green jumper joins pin 6 to the sensor's Echo row. The Arduino measures the returning pulse length.
part_guide.wire_sensor_ground: This black jumper joins the sensor's GND row to the top-edge ground rail. It completes the sensor's power and signal reference.
part_guide.wire_buzzer_signal: This blue jumper joins pin 8 to the piezo's positive row. It carries the alternating signal that makes each beep.
part_guide.wire_buzzer_ground: This black jumper joins the piezo's negative row to the top-edge ground rail. It completes the buzzer circuit.

tests.title: Test the red LED
tests.what_it_tests: This proves that the red LED, current-limiting resistor, and ground connections are complete and properly oriented.
tests.code: void setup() { pinMode(13, OUTPUT); } void loop() { digitalWrite(13, HIGH); delay(500); digitalWrite(13, LOW); delay(500); }
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. The red LED on the breadboard should blink on and off once every second.
tests.if_not: Check if the LED is backwards in Step 3 (longer leg in row 10, shorter leg in row 11). Check resistor placement in row 11 and row 15 (Step 4). Re-check the ground wire from Arduino GND to the rail (Step 7), the orange jumper from pin 13 to row 10, column a (Step 8), and the black wire from row 15, column a to the ground rail (Step 9).

tests.title: Test the ultrasonic sensor
tests.what_it_tests: This proves that the ultrasonic distance sensor is correctly powered, grounded, and measuring distance.
tests.code: const byte TRIG_PIN = 7; const byte ECHO_PIN = 6; void setup() { Serial.begin(9600); pinMode(TRIG_PIN, OUTPUT); pinMode(ECHO_PIN, INPUT); } void loop() { digitalWrite(TRIG_PIN, LOW); delayMicroseconds(2); digitalWrite(TRIG_PIN, HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10); digitalWrite(TRIG_PIN, LOW); unsigned long echoTime = pulseIn(ECHO_PIN, HIGH, 25000UL); float distanceCm = echoTime * 0.0343f / 2.0f; Serial.print("Distance: "); Serial.print(distanceCm); Serial.println(" cm"); delay(200); }
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. Open the Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. You should see distance readings updating five times a second that decrease as you move your hand closer to the sensor.
tests.if_not: Check the ultrasonic sensor pin alignment across rows 24 through 27 in Step 5 (VCC in row 24, Trig in row 25, Echo in row 26, GND in row 27). Check the 5V power jumper to row 24, column a (Step 10), trigger jumper on pin 7 to row 25, column a (Step 11), echo jumper on pin 6 to row 26, column a (Step 12), and ground jumper from row 27, column a to the top ground rail (Step 13).

assumptions: No existing parts or placements were specified, so all required items are added.
The breadboard's outer rail along the top edge, above column a, is the blue (-) ground rail and is continuous along its length. No positive power rail is used.
The sensor has a fitted male header whose printed pin order is VCC, Trig, Echo, GND and which can plug into four consecutive breadboard rows.
Use a low-current passive piezo suitable for direct GPIO drive, not an active or magnetic buzzer.
Gently form the piezo leads to reach the specified holes without stressing the body.
Scene board sizes use the required rendering templates; the physical Uno body is 68.6 by 53.4 mm.
The LED resistor is on the cathode side to follow the specified layout; it limits the same series current as a resistor on the anode side.

placements.where: row 27, column a, on the a-through-e side of the centre gap

placements.what: Black sensor ground wire end B
placements.where: the ground rail along the top edge, the outer blue (-) line, next to row 27

steps.check: A black jumper joins column a, row 27, to the outer top-edge ground rail beside row 27; sensor GND occupies the same connected row.

steps.title: Connect the buzzer signal
steps.instruction: Connect a blue jumper from the Arduino digital header pin labelled 8 to row 40, column a, on the breadboard.

placements.what: Blue buzzer signal wire end A
placements.where: Arduino digital header pin labelled 8

placements.what: Blue buzzer signal wire end B
placements.where: row 40, column a, on the a-through-e side of the centre gap

steps.check: The blue jumper joins Arduino pin 8 to column a, row 40, sharing a connected row with the piezo's + lead.

steps.title: Ground the buzzer
steps.instruction: Connect a black jumper from row 43, column a, up to the ground rail along the top edge next to row 43.

placements.what: Black buzzer ground wire end A
placements.where: row 43, column a, on the a-through-e side of the centre gap

placements.what: Black buzzer ground wire end B
placements.where: the ground rail along the top edge, the outer blue (-) line, next to row 43

steps.check: A black jumper joins column a, row 43, to the outer top-edge ground rail beside row 43, completing the piezo's negative connection.

plan.final_result: The finished breadboard has one red LED and resistor near row 10, the ultrasonic sensor near rows 24–27, and the piezo near rows 40–43, with nine jumper wires. With the sketch running, an object within 100 cm produces short beeps that become more frequent as it approaches. Below 10 cm the external red LED lights; the Uno's built-in pin-13 LED may light too. No echo or a distance beyond 100 cm produces silence and an unlit warning LED.
safety: Keep USB and any other power disconnected while placing or changing components.
Before applying USB power, verify the sensor's printed VCC and GND labels and check that 5V is not connected to the ground rail.
Keep the 220 ohm resistor in series with the LED; never connect the LED directly between D13 and ground.
Use a low-current passive piezo suitable for direct Arduino GPIO drive. A magnetic buzzer, speaker or higher-current sounder requires a driver circuit instead.
Do not force a sensor header with a different pin order into this layout; the printed labels must match the listed placements.
The HC-SR04 has a minimum useful range of about 2 cm and may miss angled, soft or narrow objects. This is a learning project, not a vehicle safety system.
